items.title: Shifting Enrollments from CS to "AI-Resistant" and Hardware Fields
items.summary: The 2026 Stanford Human-Centered AI Index reports an 11% drop in undergraduate computer science enrollments, with students increasingly shifting toward perceived "AI-resistant" engineering disciplines (like mechanical, electrical, and biomedical) that integrate physical hardware with software where AI cannot easily replace human oversight.

items.title: Why Humanities Majors Are 2026’s Stealth Power Players In Tech
items.summary: The rapid automation of technical tasks has diminished sole reliance on standard STEM coding skills, creating a surge in demand for workers who can bridge the "AI translation gap" using communication, empathy, and strategic storytelling.

items.title: Top STEM Jobs for AI Career Advancement
items.summary: Despite soft hiring in general sectors, specialized AI and machine learning engineering roles are projected to grow up to 40% through the decade, with employers struggling to find skilled applicants and offering workers with AI skills a 56% wage premium over non-AI technical roles.

items.title: Employer MBA Hiring Trends & AI Skills for 2026
items.summary: A survey of 500 hiring managers revealed that 22% now view AI proficiency as a baseline expectation for MBA-level roles rather than a differentiator, with "AI fluency" ranking as the single most valued skill (35%) ahead of the ability to quantify business impact.

items.title: The Rise of the "Two-Track" Business Labor Market
items.summary: Analyzing over a billion job advertisements, the report highlights a "two-track" market where business roles "professionalized" by AI are growing twice as fast and command 42% higher wage growth, with junior business roles increasingly requiring traditionally senior human skills like leadership.

items.title: Demand for AI Skills in Entry-level Jobs Nearly Triples Since Fall 2025
items.source: National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE)
items.summary: The Job Outlook Spring Update survey found that more than one-third of all entry-level jobs now require AI skills—nearly tripling the rate reported in late 2025—making AI literacy a critical component for graduating business majors entering the workforce.

items.title: Why Humanities Majors Are 2026’s Stealth Power Players In Tech
items.summary: As generative AI increasingly automates technical coding and software tasks, companies are placing a higher premium on "soft degrees." LinkedIn workforce data reveals that social science and humanities majors are finding clearer career paths in the tech sector than specialized junior engineers, leveraging human-centric skills like branding, stakeholder empathy, storytelling, and bridging the "AI translation gap."

items.title: 2026 AI, Automation, and the Future of Sociology Degree Careers
items.summary: Recent labor studies indicate that 45% of sociology-related jobs now require proficiency in AI-enhanced data interpretation, automating routine database management and survey coding while driving social science graduates toward specialized roles in AI-supported health analysis, qualitative research, and public policy.

items.title: Lower-skilled workers could earn more in an AI world
items.summary: Research by Stanford economist Lukas Althoff indicates that while AI will help elevate lower-skilled workers by simplifying complex tasks, traditional degrees intensive in verbal and social skills—such as political science and sociology—may face more severe market disruption and slower wage growth compared to technical, physical, or applied trades.
